item.title: NP-Completeness of the Three-Dimensional Polyhedral Separation Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.28644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bone tumor resection planning motivates the following geometric problem. Given tumor points and healthy-bone points in three-dimensional space, find cutting planes that separate the tumor from the surrounding bone. To avoid tumor seeding, the cutting planes must not pass through the tumor. Given a positive integer k, select at most k closed halfspaces whose intersection contains all tumor points, while minimizing the total weight of healthy-bone points strictly inside this intersection. We formalize this problem and prove that its threshold decision version is NP-complete. Consequently, the corresponding optimization problem is NP-hard.
item.dc:creator: Guannan Guo

item.title: Turing Completeness of Greedy UNO with an Ultimately Periodic Infinite Deck
item.description: arXiv:2611.29739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We encode an arbitrary two-counter Minsky machine as a two-player UNO round with an ultimately periodic infinite draw pile $uw^\omega$. The construction uses a fixed $17$-card prefix and a period of length quadratic in the number of instructions. When both players follow the same fixed greedy policy, the round terminates exactly when the machine halts, and every available hand play has a unique card type. Consequently, greedy termination and victory by a designated player -- as well as winning-strategy existence under forced-play rules without tie-breaking -- are $\Sigma^0_1$-complete. Under official voluntary-draw rules with unrestricted legal choices, however, the existence of a finite play is decidable (and primitive recursive) via reachability in fixed-dimension vector addition systems with states (VASS). Finally, the maximal duration of a finite greedy play has no total computable upper bound in the input length.
item.dc:creator: T. V. Kuptsov (Lomonosov Moscow State University), G. A. Khaziev (Institute for Information Transmission Problems RAS, Central University)

item.title: Unshardable Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.29925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.
item.dc:creator: Prashanth Amireddy, Yevgeniy Dodis, Rohan Goyal, Ethan Mook, Madhu Sudan, Daniel Wichs

item.title: How Much Randomness is Needed to Convert MA Protocols to AM Protocols?
item.description: arXiv:2611.30127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Merlin-Arthur class of languages MA is included into Arthur-Merlin class AM, and into PP. For a standard transformation of a given MA protocol with Arthur's message (= random string) of length a and Merlin's message of length m to a PP machine, the latter needs O(ma)random bits. The same holds for simulating MA protocols by AM protocols: in the resulting AM protocol the length of Arthur's message (= random string) is O(ma). And the same holds for simulating heuristic MA protocols by heuristic AM protocols as well. In the paper [A.Knop, Circuit Lower Bounds for Average-Case MA, CSR 2015] it was conjectured that, in the transformation of heuristic MA protocols to heuristic AM protocols, O(ma) can be replaced by a polynomial of a only. A similar question can be asked for normal MA and AM protocols, and for the simulation of MA protocols by PP machines. In the present paper we show that, relative to an oracle, both latter questions answer in the negative and Knop's conjecture is false. Moreover, the same is true for simulation of MA protocols by AM protocols in which the error probability is not bounded away from 1/2, the so called PP.NP protocols. The latter protocols generalize both AM protocols and PP machines.
item.dc:creator: Nikolay Vereshchagin

item.title: Optimal XOR Lemmas for Information Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.30432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information complexity studies how much information the parties to a communication protocol must reveal to each other about their inputs to accomplish a given task. For a Boolean-valued communication problem $F$, let ${\rm IC}_\epsilon(F)$ denote its information complexity with error $\epsilon$, and let $F^{\oplus n}$ denote the XOR of $n$ independent instances of $F$. A fundamental question is whether information complexity obeys an XOR lemma, ${\rm IC}_{1/3}(F^{\oplus n})=\Omega(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{1/(3n)}(F))$, which would match the trivial upper bound. Previous work either established the $n$-fold increase in information cost without the $n$-fold decrease in error (Bar-Yossef et al., FOCS 2002) or proved a lower bound with a subtracted penalty proportional to the input length of $F$ (Sawettamalya and Yu, STOC 2025). In particular, the question has remained open even for the XOR of $n$ or fewer copies of a function $F:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$. We completely resolve the question of XOR lemmas for information complexity, for every error $0\le\epsilon\le1/3$. For total functions $F$, we prove that ${\rm IC}_\epsilon(F^{\oplus n})=\Theta(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{\epsilon/n}(F))$ unless $F$ has the degenerate form $F(x,y)=a(x)\oplus b(y)$, in which case ${\rm IC}_\epsilon(F^{\oplus n})=O(1)$. For the richer class of partial functions, we obtain the characterization ${\rm IC}_\epsilon(F^{\oplus n})=\Theta({\rm IC}_\epsilon(F)+n\cdot{\rm SIC}_{\epsilon/n}(F))$, where ${\rm SIC}$ is the information complexity of protocols in which Alice and Bob privately output bits whose XOR is the answer. Finally, we prove an optimal distributional XOR lemma, for every function $F$ and every distribution. We obtain an optimal direct sum theorem to accompany each of our XOR lemmas. All implicit constants are absolute. Our work contributes a novel combination of information-theoretic and geometric techniques.
item.dc:creator: Alexander A. Sherstov

item.title: A $(17/7-o(1))n$ Circuit Lower Bound for Binary-Encoded 3-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.30887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We strengthen the elementary $n-1$ circuit lower bound for a specified binary encoding of 3-SAT to $(17/7)n-O(n\log\log n/\log n)$ gates over the full two-input Boolean basis, with unrestricted depth and sharing. For each integer $w\ge5$, we encode 3-CNF formulas with exactly $m=2^w-1$ clauses over $m$ available variables using $n=3m(w+1)$ bits. The proof embeds Boolean tests in variable identifiers while retaining $n-o(n)$ free bits, and combines weighted gate elimination with a nonlinear-gate lower bound from the tests' full algebraic degree over $\mathbb F_2$. We provide Lean proofs of the finite inequality and the asymptotic bound for arbitrary acyclic binary circuits.
item.dc:creator: Theodoros Yianni, Sahibzada Allahyar

item.title: $\mathrm{LogCFL} = \mathrm{UAux}\bigl(O(\log n),\mathrm{poly}(n)\bigr)$
item.description: arXiv:2611.30892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We observe that the isolation technique introduced by Hoza in his proof of $\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}$ extends to give $\mathrm{LogCFL}=\mathrm{UAux}(O(\log n),\mathrm{poly}(n))$.
item.dc:creator: A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran

item.title: Separating Kolmogorov-Loveland randomness from Martin-L\"of randomness
item.description: arXiv:2611.31004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Martin-L\"of randomness requires an infinite binary sequence to pass every effective statistical test for fair coin tosses. Kolmogorov-Loveland randomness requires every computable betting strategy to have bounded capital, even when earlier answers guide its choice of which unread bit to bet on next. We prove that Martin-L\"of randomness is strictly stronger. We construct a probability measure by imposing parity equations on infinitely many disjoint finite blocks. The systems have short descriptions relative to their ranks, so every sequence in the support fails one fixed Martin-L\"of test. Almost every sequence under this measure is Kolmogorov-Loveland random. To prove this, we choose each block from a list in which every position occurs in only a small fraction of the candidates. For each betting strategy, after a normalization that preserves success, this sparsity ensures that the sum of its wager fractions on bits forced by the equations and earlier answers is almost surely finite.
item.dc:creator: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng

item.title: Connecting \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} and \textsc{Exact Cover by $k$-Sets}: A complete complexity classification of \textsc{$k$-Partitioned 1-in-3-SAT} for planar, linear and $3$-connected instances
item.description: arXiv:2611.31145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In \textsc{$k$-Partitioned 1-in-3-Sat}, the clauses of a positive \textsc{1-in-3-Sat} formula are partitioned into~$k$ classes such that every variable occurs exactly once in each class. This problem corresponds to \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} restricted to instances in which every element lies in exactly three tuples. For every~$k$, we provide a complete complexity classification with respect to all combinations of three structural restrictions on the incidence graph: planarity, linearity (no two clauses share more than one variable) and 3-connectivity. We show \textsc{NP}-completeness of \textsc{$3$-Partitioned 1-in-3-Sat} and \#\textsc{P}-completeness of its counting version, which also serve as a starting point for the further reductions, and then enforce the desired properties by repeatedly inserting gadgets into the incidence graph. As a consequence, we obtain that \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} and \textsc{Exact Cover by $k$-Sets} remain \textsc{NP}-hard under the same restrictions, even if every element occurs in exactly three tuples or sets, respectively. In particular, \textsc{Planar $4$-Dimensional Matching} is \textsc{NP}-complete and we complement the \textsc{NP}-hardness result with an \textsc{FPT} algorithm with respect to the number of so-called quadrilateral components of a given plane embedding of the incidence graph.
item.dc:creator: Janosch D\"ocker, Britta Dorn, Hannah Van Santvliet, Katrin Willger

item.title: Deterministic regularisation of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem
item.description: arXiv:2611.28614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm for pseudospectral shattering in exact arithmetic. This resolves an important open problem in the complexity of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem. Given a complex contraction $A$ of order $n\ge2$ and $0<\delta<1/2$, we compute a perturbation $E$ with $\|E\|<\delta$ such that $A+E$ has simple spectrum. The ratio of its eigenbasis condition number to its minimum eigenvalue gap is at most $C(n/\delta)^{20/3}$. The algorithm also computes an exact eigensystem of $A+E$. It uses $O(n^3\log^d(n/\delta))$ real-field operations and comparisons, where $C$ and $d$ are absolute constants. We choose the rank-one perturbations using a lower bound on the circle mean of the logarithm of the discriminant modulus. A quadratic penalty controls how far the accumulated updates move the matrix. By using the same reference eigenbasis for several updates, we can estimate all the current projector norms while recovering only the directions needed for the next perturbation.
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Colbrook

item.title: Two Primes Suffice for Definable Graph Canonisation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study inflationary fixed-point logic on finite simple graphs with unordered vertices and an ordered number sort. For a prime $r$, the quantifier $M_r$ tests whether the number of relations satisfying a formula is nonzero modulo $r$. For any distinct primes $p$ and $q$, the logic with $M_p$ and $M_q$ defines the adjacency matrix of a canonical copy on the number sort. On labelled inputs this matrix is computable in deterministic polynomial time with an oracle that tests whether the number of satisfying assignments of a Boolean circuit is nonzero modulo $p$. For each prime $p$, the logic with $M_p$ alone cannot define a canonical copy on all graphs. The primes also differ on Boolean queries. There is a single first-order formula $\beta(S)$ on vertex sets such that $M_q S \beta(S)$ is undefinable with $M_p$ alone whenever $p \ne q$. For a positive integer-valued function $g$, consider the class of all graphs $G$ with at most $g(|V(G)|)$ automorphisms. For each fixed prime $p$, the logic with $M_p$ canonises this class exactly when $g$ is bounded.
item.dc:creator: Vaani Goenka, Aalok Thakkar

item.title: Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.30657v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.
item.dc:creator: Paco Navarro, Michael Emmerich

item.title: How Do Deep Networks Encode and Selectively Use Information? Shared Encoding and Conditional Signed Readout in Vision and Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.30854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How can trained deep networks retain contextual information across internal representations while using it selectively in a decision? We study this question through controlled background-texture edits in vision classifiers and entity-binding edits in frozen language models. Across both modalities, factor perturbations preserve recognizable structure across pre-fixed, mutually disjoint blocks of hidden units: visual channel blocks match their complements more closely for the same image than for other images under the same texture edit, while language blocks transfer a relational direction fitted under one query role to rank relational states within held-out name pairs under the other role. We then decompose the local output change into signed channel and pathway contributions. In a convolutional classifier, net channel-level reinforcement ($R^{(512)}>1$) coexists on individual images with cancellation between positive- and negative-weight groups ($R^{(2)}<1$). Holding weights, the paired relation edit, and red/blue answer words fixed, switching prompt presentation reverses the mean finite selection effect in Qwen2.5. Two held-out tests validate this mechanism. Attenuating development-selected antagonistic units amplifies edit effects on unseen inputs; in a vision transformer, attenuating the same frozen units in one forward pass increases the mean magnitude of the background-edit effect on one class margin and reduces it on another, with the opposite pattern for a second group (four-cell paired interaction $+78.30\times 10^{-5}$ logit). Finally, combining conditional channel variance with fixed downstream readout weights predicts single-channel pruning recovery across ten cuts. These results show how shared encoding and conditional signed readout can coexist in vision and language models.
item.dc:creator: Kaixiang Shu

item.title: Two messages suffice for quantum interactive proof systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.31236v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum interactive proof systems can be parallelized to three messages, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), perhaps their most striking distinction from classical counterparts. In this work, we establish that any quantum interactive proof system can further be parallelized to two messages, with the verifier sending halves of EPR pairs (``quantum public coins'') and, after the prover's response, using only stoquastic verification. Technically, we strengthen ${\sf QIP}(3) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}$ of Jain, Ji, Upadhyay, and Watrous (JACM, 2011) and fully characterize two-message quantum interactive proof systems by proving \[ {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf StoqAM} = {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM} = {\sf QIP}(2) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}. \] Our main technical contributions show that Close Image to Uniform (CIUniform), which is naturally in the stoquastic version of ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$, is $\sf PSPACE$-hard via transforming the sum-check protocol of Shamir (JACM, 1992) and Shen (JACM, 1992) into a CIUniform instance consisting of an efficient sampler whose image distribution is exactly uniform for some input distribution when the underlying quantified Boolean formula is true.
item.dc:creator: Yupan Liu

item.title: The Swap Median and Swap Closest Problems are NP-complete for Three Permutations
item.description: arXiv:2409.09734v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The swap distance (or Cayley distance) between two permutations is the minimum number of exchanges of two elements transforming one into the other. Given three permutations, Swap Median asks for a permutation minimizing the sum of the swap distances to the inputs, and Swap Closest asks for one minimizing the maximum distance. Both problems are NP-hard for an unbounded number of inputs, but the case of three inputs, the smallest non-trivial one, has remained open. We prove that both problems are NP-complete for three permutations. Swap Median remains NP-complete even when two of the inputs differ by disjoint swaps. For Swap Closest, it is already NP-complete to decide whether the trivial lower bound is attained. Along the way, we show that finding a permutation lying on shortest paths from one input to each of the other two, as far as possible from that input, is NP-hard and APX-hard. We also characterize when the triangle-inequality lower bound of the median is attained, and we give a quadratic-time algorithm when cycles are short, which yields a dichotomy. Finally, experiments on simulated evolutionary data show that a simple certified heuristic is optimal on all small instances and recovers ancestral permutations.
item.dc:creator: Lu\'is Cunha, Thiago Lopes, Arnaud Mary

item.title: nni+: a local subtree-move distance for mutation trees
item.description: arXiv:2501.07529v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mutation trees describe the order in which somatic mutations accumulate in a tumor. Inference from noisy sequencing data yields many plausible trees, so comparing mutation trees is a basic task, and a distance is most useful when its value has a direct evolutionary meaning. Rearrangement distances have this meaning: they count how many local corrections separate two evolutionary histories. However, the classical local move, the nearest neighbor interchange (NNI), does not suit mutation trees, where every node carries a mutation, because it preserves the number of children of every node and so cannot connect all trees. We propose nni+, which moves a set of sibling subtrees one level up or down and corresponds to stating that a mutation occurred before or after a group of subclones branched off. We compare it with its elementary version, which moves one subtree at a time, and with the rotation-free generalized NNI (gNNI), which exchanges subtrees across an edge in both directions. We show that nni+ induces a metric with diameter 2n-2, and we give a 2-approximation for nni+ and for gNNI. Our main result is that the nni+ distance has an exact formula and can be computed in polynomial time, whereas both the elementary distance and the rotation-free gNNI distance are NP-complete. The key is to view a mutation tree as a family of compatible clusters, in which every move replaces a single cluster. For the elementary distance we also characterize, by a linear-time test, when it coincides with the parent--child distance.
item.dc:creator: Lu\'is Cunha, Jack Kuipers, Thiago Lopes

item.title: The Solver's Paradox for SAT
item.description: arXiv:2511.14665v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show in Rocq that every circuit verifier $v$ determines a formula $\psi_v$ whose satisfiability is $v$'s acceptance of its own diagonal claim: a satisfiability predicate thus behaves like a provability predicate. Every solver represented in the language misclassifies its own diagonal instance, and every verifier misjudges its own diagonal claim. We distinguish our result from (i) the refuters of Chen et al. (2024), which produce from the description of a solver an instance it gets wrong, and (ii) the refuter of Gutfreund et al. (2007) for efficient SAT solvers, which needs a hardness hypothesis and a simulation. Here the refuter is purely syntactic, and it separates evaluation of the language from its own expressions, not SAT from a resource-bounded class. The identity behind the fixed point uses no property of quotation; its reading as self-reference depends on the coding, and an injective recoding flips the branch. A truth table decides $\psi_v$ only from outside the language. Written inside, it is brute force: it settles the claim from above and has a diagonal instance of its own. This yields an unconditional certification hierarchy with tower growth, a quadratic lower bound on every internal evaluator, and an exponential lower bound on brute force.
item.dc:creator: Milan Rosko

item.title: Constant-Coin Complete-Information Debates for $\mathsf{P}$ with Arbitrarily Small Strong Error
item.description: arXiv:2609.24272v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study complete-information debate systems in which a probabilistic finite-state verifier reads the alternating messages of a prover and a refuter. Demirci, Say, and Yakary{\i}lmaz showed that every language in $\mathsf{P}$ has such debates checkable with a constant number of random bits and arbitrarily small weak error. Their strong-error construction, which also counts nontermination as failure, did not permit arbitrary error reduction. We close this gap: for every $L\in\mathsf{P}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant-space verifier using a constant number of private coin tosses that has perfect completeness and strong error at most $\varepsilon$. The verifier simulates a polynomial-time alternating multihead finite automaton, privately spot-checking one of its input heads. The key observation is that, on a nonmember, the refuter may concede any round in which the prover first misreports a head reading. This ensures termination against every prover when the refuter follows the specified strategy, and permits strong-error reduction by repetition.
item.dc:creator: M. Utkan Gezer

item.title: Randomized, Quantum and Postselected Multitape Time in Deterministic Space t/sqrt(log t)
item.description: arXiv:2611.01884v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that a bounded-error multitape Turing machine running in time $t$ can be simulated deterministically in space $O(t/\sqrt{\log t})$, with no constructibility assumption on $t$. The simulation computes any bit of the exact number of accepting coin strings, so it also covers majority, postselected, nondeterministic and modular acceptance. It uses the tensor-network contraction behind the recent refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which Cruz used to put nondeterministic time $T$ in space $T(\log\log T)^2/\sqrt{\log T}$. Our space accounting removes the $(\log\log T)^2$ factor. Writing a pair of quantum paths as one weighted classical run, we obtain the same bound for bounded-error quantum time with polynomial-time computable amplitudes, for postselected quantum time with algebraic amplitudes, and for quantum Merlin-Arthur time with witnesses of $O(t/(\log t)^{3/2})$ qubits. For explicit circuits, acceptance probabilities of $S$-gate quantum circuits and #CircuitSAT for $S$-gate Boolean circuits are computed exactly in space $O(S/\sqrt{\log S})$ plus the logarithm of the description length. As consequences, for every constant $K$ some language in deterministic linear space differs, at every large input length, from every bounded-error or postselected quantum machine running in time $o(n\sqrt{\log n})$ with $Kn$ bits of advice; another has correlation $O((\log n)/\sqrt{n})$ with every randomized or algebraic-amplitude quantum machine of that time with $\log^2 n$ bits of advice; and DSPACE$(n)$ is not contained in BPTIME$[o(n\sqrt{\log n})]$ with constant-length advice that may depend on the coins. Finally, exact counting or postselected simulation in space $T^{1-\varepsilon}$ would refute the Weak Exponential Time Hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Ben Daniel

item.title: Nondeterministic Space and Time from Backward Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.16779v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A discovery made late in one run can guide another from its first step. We let a deterministic program pass a finite register between runs on the same input. An observer follows one run forward or moves back to an earlier step of a fresh run, which starts with the register contents of the step just left. We call this handoff backward feedback. The step number in view is a random clock whose proposed changes are independent draws from a fixed distribution with bounded jumps of both signs and negative mean. At equilibrium, every stationary distribution of the clock and register must give the correct bit almost surely. For each fixed polynomial bound on time and register length, feedback gives nondeterministic space at that bound. Disabling feedback gives deterministic time, a strictly smaller class. Their unions are $\mathbf{PSPACE}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. Starting from a blank register, an observer must see acceptance by a deadline counted in clock ticks, with uniformly positive probability on members and never on nonmembers. Subexponential deadlines then give exactly the languages determined by a bounded input prefix. Take a deadline exponential in a fixed polynomial bound. If no initial register may lead a nonmember to acceptance, the observable class is nondeterministic time at that bound with feedback and deterministic time without it. The separation is unconditional for linear bounds, and the unions are $\mathbf{NP}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. If only the blank start must be safe, the union with feedback is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$, as at equilibrium. A clock that takes single steps and favors moving back seldom gets far into a run, so a message ready late takes longer to send. Clearing a saved count means waiting for all the handoffs needed to fill it again.
item.dc:creator: Saman Farhat, Farzad Didehvar

item.title: What Can Postselection on Halting Decide?
item.description: arXiv:2611.20517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A probabilistic program can produce an answer on some runs and continue forever on others. Suppose it halts with positive probability on every input and we count only the runs that halt. Aaronson et al. showed that if the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one, such programs decide exactly the problems solvable with a finite list of halting questions chosen in advance. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be more likely than the wrong one. We prove that the resulting class is exactly $\boldsymbol{\Delta^0_2}$: the halting questions can now be asked one at a time, with each answer helping to determine the next question. This remains true if the program must halt with probability at least 99%, or with any other prescribed rational lower bound below one. Our main technical result is the exact query bound when the program gives two guarantees. Suppose it halts with probability at least $\rho$ and, among the runs that halt, the correct answer has probability at least $a$. For rational $0 < \rho < 1$ and $1/2 < a < 1$, these programs decide exactly the problems solvable with at most $n$ halting questions chosen in advance, where $n$ is the largest integer satisfying $\rho(a/(1-a))^n \le 1$. Every value of $n$ occurs, and different values give different classes. The proof measures how much additional halting probability a change of answer requires, and counts these changes as in Ershov's hierarchy. The results extend to quantum machines with computable gates.
item.dc:creator: Saman Farhat, Farzad Didehvar

item.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
item.description: arXiv:2611.26169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.
item.dc:creator: John Paul Steinberger, Zhe Zhang

item.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2511.03752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
item.dc:creator: Rick van der Heijden

item.title: On Big-M Reformulations of Bilevel Linear Programs: Hardness of A Posteriori Verification
item.description: arXiv:2603.17107v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A standard approach to solving optimistic bilevel linear programs (BLPs) is to replace the lower-level problem with its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions and reformulate the resulting complementarity constraints using auxiliary binary variables. This yields a single-level mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model involving big-$M$ parameters. While sufficiently large big-$M$s that preserve at least one bilevel-optimal solution can be computed in polynomial time, verifying a priori that given big-$M$s do not cut off any feasible or optimal lower-level solutions is known to be computationally difficult. In this paper, we establish two complementary hardness results. First, we show that, even with a single potentially incorrect big-$M$ parameter, it is coNP-complete to verify a posteriori whether a given optimal solution of the resulting MILP model is bilevel optimal. In particular, this negative result persists for min-max problems without coupling constraints and applies to strong-duality-based reformulations of mixed-integer BLPs. Second, we show that verifying global big-$M$ correctness remains computationally difficult a posteriori, even when an optimal solution of the MILP model is available.
item.dc:creator: Sergey S. Ketkov, Oleg A. Prokopyev

item.title: Polynomial-Time Optimal Group Selection via the Double-Commutator Eigenvalue Problem
item.description: arXiv:2605.00834v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The algebraic diversity framework generalizes temporal averaging over multiple observations to algebraic group action on a single observation for second-order statistical estimation. The central open problem in this framework is $\textit{group selection}$: given an $M$-dimensional observation with unknown covariance structure, find the finite group whose spectral decomposition best matches the covariance. Naive enumeration of all subgroups of the symmetric group $S_M$ requires exponential time in $M$. We prove that this combinatorial problem, restricted to a basis of $d$ candidate generators, reduces to a generalized eigenvalue problem derived from the double commutator of the covariance matrix, with complexity $O(d^2M^2 + d^3)$ for sparse (permutation-type) generators and $O(d^2M^3 + d^3)$ in general. The minimum eigenvector gives the optimal generator in the span of the basis in closed form, with no iterative optimization. The minimum eigenvalue is zero if and only if a generator in the span commutes exactly with the covariance, and its magnitude is a certifiable optimality gap otherwise. The problem does not appear in the standard catalog of Garey and Johnson (1979) and links group theory, matrix analysis, and statistical estimation. We relate it to independent component analysis (JADE), structured matrix nearness, and simultaneous diagonalization, and show that the double-commutator form is the unique objective, up to scale, built from a unitarily invariant quadratic norm of the commutator. We extend the framework to non-Abelian symmetry recovery via a Sequential GEVP with deflation, which is sound but not always complete, give canonical generator sets whose direct testing is complete for five named group families, and add two identifiability theorems on the commutant-lattice ambiguity and on whether $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf{R})$ recovers a generative subgroup or only a supergroup.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: Extending CDCL to disjunctions of parity equations
item.description: arXiv:2605.15002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Problems provably hard for Resolution are also provably hard for CDCL, but shorter proofs can sometimes be found using stronger proof systems such as Res($\oplus$), a generalization of Resolution to XNF formulas, whose constraints are disjunctions of parity equations, called linear clauses. While some solvers like CryptoMiniSat reason on Boolean clauses with separate parity equations in a system called CNF-XOR, general XNF reasoning is less explored. We present CDCL($\oplus$), a generalization of CDCL to XNF formulas that includes branching on arbitrary parity equations, linear-algebraic reasoning during unit propagation, and learning linear clauses in conflict analysis. Our key tool is the affine resolution rule, which generalizes classical resolution and allows translations of 1-UIP clause learning and variable elimination. We develop a theory of UIPs to show that we learn an asserting clause with the largest possible backjump, the same guarantee as classical CDCL. We prove that CDCL($\oplus$) not only produces Res($\oplus$) proofs, but also polynomially simulates Res($\oplus$) given nondeterministic decisions and restarts, much like the relationship between CDCL and Resolution. We implement CDCL($\oplus$) in our solver Xorcle, which cleanly adapts over a dozen major classical CDCL heuristics. We introduce the CSIDS decision heuristic, which selects decisions from activity-ranked clauses, and the LRUP($\oplus$) proof logging format. On a suite of cryptographic benchmarks, Xorcle is generally competitive with or outperforms Kissat, CaDiCaL, and CryptoMiniSat, and beats the concurrently developed XNF solver Xorricane. Additionally, Xorcle's reasoning and search alone (i.e., without detecting XORs) solves CNF versions of Tseitin formulas, perfect matching formulas, and bijective pigeonhole formulas with $n+1$ pigeons into $n$ holes using apparently polynomial running time.
item.dc:creator: Paul Beame, Glenn Sun

item.title: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
item.description: arXiv:2610.21216v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the n parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a $(1-o(1))n\log n$ lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$, which is known to be tight. As a consequence, we obtain the same lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$. We also prove an $\Omega(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$. An alternative proof technique recovers most of these bounds as well as the previously known approach based on Nechiporuk's method. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private and support private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}(n)$ respectively for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$ and $MOD_q$ with prime $q$, the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors. Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a $\omega(n)$ lower bound for $OR_n$ using the same approach as our alternative technique. Both works used substantial AI assistance.
item.dc:creator: Marshall Ball, Peter Crawford-Kahrl, Vladimir Podolskii, Morgan Prior

item.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
item.description: arXiv:2610.40535v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi

item.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
item.description: arXiv:2611.26080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We survey bounds that can be recovered from earlier work under FPT $\neq$ W[1] and prove seven lower bounds for graph problems and set systems under the same assumption. The new proofs encode clique choices in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of the encoding. This lets us turn a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem into a fixed-parameter algorithm for Clique or Multicolored Clique. In several cases, the new bound matches the function of the parameter in the historical exponent, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.
item.dc:creator: Hendrik Molter
